shortened: May the light shining from the Most Exalted Center and the All-Glorious Kingdom descend upon your pure spirit, your radiant body, and your illumined grave, and envelop your darkened resting place, O glorious martyr and sacrificial offering in the path of your Lord, the Merciful, the Compassionate.

order.why: Extend remembrance across the hours of day and night.
shortened: Well is it with thee and with whosoever visiteth thy resting-place at dawn and eventide, in the daytime and the night season. This, verily, is but a token of the grace of thine incomparable Lord.

order.why: Keep the invitation to seek, visit and recite.
shortened: Blessed is the seeker who seeks your tomb, and the lover who visits your grave and recites what the tongue of your Lord has uttered.

order.why: Link visitation with the remembrance of virtues.
shortened: Blessed is he who speaketh in praise of thee, who remembereth thy sacrifice and virtuous qualities, who visiteth thy resting-place and reciteth that which hath been sent down from the Pen of Grace in the Most Great Prison.

order.why: Read the written mention as an aid to visitation.
Turn to the account of a Tablet revealed after a believer’s passing.
shortened: The Ancient Beauty was well pleased with 'Abdu's-Salih, and after his ascension revealed a Visitation Tablet in his honor, also delivering an address concerning him, which was taken down and published together with other Scriptures.

order.why: Read the significance assigned to receiving a special Visitation Tablet.
shortened: In truth, he ended his days in trials and tribulations in the path of God, drank from the cup of every affliction and tasted the poison of every ordeal until he reached a station that became the envy of the chosen ones, and a special Visitation Tablet was revealed from the Supreme Pen. No bounty equals or parallels this favor. That Visitation Tablet was recited and the special grace and bounty became clear and evident.

order.why: An opening passage of a Tablet of visitation honoring a martyr.
Retain the named identification of a prayer.
shortened: O steadfast one in the Covenant! This is the visitation prayer for His Holiness Mirza Isma'il Khayyat. The friends must each recite it on behalf of 'Abdu'l-Baha with complete detachment, attraction, and burning with the fire of the love of God.

order.why: Keep the account of writing a Tablet for a resting place.
shortened: O My trusted one! Thou knowest how devoted a soul was His Holiness Ismu'llah al-Asdaq, upon him be the Glory of God, the Most Glorious, and to what extent he served the Sacred Threshold, and how pure, sincere and radiant he was. Therefore 'Abdu'l-Baha penned a Tablet of Visitation for that illustrious personage, to be recited at his pure resting-place.

order.why: Observe the practical transmission of a copy for recitation.
shortened: Previously, a special visitation tablet was written specifically for that noble person, and a copy of it is being sent so that you may recite it.

order.why: Preserve the statement that a complete version would follow.
Attend to remembrance on anniversaries and on another’s behalf.
shortened: On behalf of 'Abdu'l-Baha, on the anniversary of the martyrdom of each of these two distinguished ones, if possible the friends should go to the luminous resting place of Haji and the perfumed wilderness of Hashim and recite this prayer of visitation on behalf of 'Abdu'l-Baha.

order.why: Keep the request for the friends to recite by proxy.
shortened: A prayer of visitation has been written for that martyr of the plain of trial. The divine friends should recite it on behalf of 'Abdu'l-Baha.

order.why: Connect remembrance with identifying and repairing a grave.
Let prudence and humility shape the journey.
shortened: A prayer of visitation is being written for that pure soul martyred in God's path. Some of the friends should journey with perfect wisdom to that fragrant tomb and, on behalf of Abdul-Baha, visit it with complete humility.

order.why: Keep the particular instruction concerning the visiting friends and the Tablet.
shortened: First, on behalf of 'Abdu'l-Baha, a few of the friends should visit the luminous resting place of the servant of Baha and recite this, then deliver it to Jinab-i-Mirza Baqir.

order.why: Read the request to visit the place of martyrdom.
shortened: Upon receipt of the Visitation Tablet, the loved ones of God should, on behalf of this servant, proceed to the place of martyrdom of that wronged one and recite that Visitation Tablet.

order.why: Hear the shared grief of recitation on another’s behalf.
shortened: From the longing in the heart of that spiritual friend, tears flowed in the Holy Shrine and hearts were set aflame. With weeping eyes, we collectively recited the Visitation Tablet on your behalf.

order.why: Let midnight prayer include everyone in remembrance.
shortened: I swear by your precious life that at midnight I will arise and, facing the Holy Shrine, will perform the visitation with utmost supplication and entreaty on behalf of all.

order.why: Connect visitation with assistance for teaching and service.
shortened: Yesterday I placed my face upon the Blessed Threshold and performed the visitation on your behalf and supplicated for confirmation in teaching the Cause of God.

order.why: Hear the visitor’s petition following its repeated address to God.
Close with the Báb’s priority of recognizing the living promised Manifestation.
shortened: Then if, on that Day -- on the Day of Friday -- thou shouldst stand before Him Whom God shall make manifest, blessed art thou! For He shall suffice thee in lieu of visiting the Letters of the Unity and from performing every work of righteousness. Yet though all are capable of attaining unto this, they shall deprive themselves of that supreme bounty and that most great attainment. Though they were to expend all that is upon the earth, it would not equal in recompense the weight of a single atom thereof, did they but know.

questions: How does addressing the departed differ from simply describing their lives?
What do light, fragrance, rain, and gardens convey about grief and continuing relationship?
How do visitation by proxy and the heart’s turning across distance expand the meaning of presence?
What does the graveyard greeting in Sahih Muslim illuminate, and which features belong to the particular Tablets here?
How can remembering virtues and sacrifice shape the conduct of a living community?
What does the final selection suggest about the relationship between reverence for the past and recognition of a new divine call?

references.label: 1 · Sahih Muslim 975 · Greeting and prayer at the graveyard
references.note: This narration describes Muhammad teaching a greeting for those visiting a graveyard: the departed believers are addressed in peace, the visitors acknowledge that they too will join them, and God is asked for peace for both. Compare this union of address, shared mortality, and supplication with the Visitation Tablets. The brief general greeting differs from the Tablets’ particular commemorations, testimonies, and richly varied imagery.

subjects.displayTitle: Beyond blind imitation: learning to see with one’s own eyes
subjects.introduction: The imitator, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says, reports that such a man has seen and such a man has heard; he borrows the eyes, ears and conscience of others and has no will of his own. Taqlíd, blind imitation, is that quiet surrender, and most of us practise it without noticing, since a belief inherited from parents feels less like a choice than like the weather. Bahá’u’lláh insists that the one thing conducive to the world’s reformation is that people observe and hearken with their own eyes and ears, and the Báb commands His followers to break the chains of imitation in His name. The stakes are not merely intellectual: inherited prejudice walls communities off from one another, fuels war, and has veiled every generation from the Manifestation sent to it. Yet the alternative is not the sovereignty of personal preference; the same writings forbid following one’s idle fancies. The Buddha, warning the Kálámas against trusting repetition, tradition or apparent authority and pointing them to the fruits of a teaching, describes a kindred discipline [1]. Seeing for oneself requires humility, and leads on to the independent investigation of truth, the dismantling of prejudice and superstition, and the discovery of reality itself.
subjects.arc: Begin with firsthand responsibility, examine the sources and consequences of dependence, and move toward humble inquiry and fellowship across traditions.

order.why: Describe what is lost when another’s perception replaces one’s own.
Open with the responsibility to see and hear for oneself.
Give the seeker a positive discipline of attentive investigation.
Distinguish freedom from imitation from following one’s own desires.
Calls for investigation with one’s own faculties rather than imitation of ancestors.
Connect broadened understanding with love and unity.
Make the crossing of religious barriers concrete.
shortened: Everyone must do away with false prejudices and must even go to the other churches and mosques, for, in all of these worshiping places, the name of God is mentioned. Since all gather to worship God, what difference does it make? None of these worship satan. The Mohammedans must go to the churches of the Christians and of the Jews and vice-versa, the others must go to the Mohammedan mosques. They hold aloof from one another merely because of unfounded prejudices and dogmas.

order.why: Examine inherited identity through a particular example.
shortened: Because this man's father was a Jew, he considers himself a Jew. Not that he has investigated reality and proved satisfactorily to himself that Judaism is right -- nay, rather, he is aware that his forefathers have followed this course; therefore, he has held to it himself.

order.why: Widen the criticism across several communities.
Keep the further reported account of accumulated tradition.
Identify the assumption that ancestry establishes truth.
shortened: Today the religious leaders suppose that religion consists of blind imitation of one's ancestors. Therefore each people clings to its traditions and considers them to be true.

order.why: Connect inherited belief with misinterpretation of scripture.
shortened: Misconception of the Word of God and its meanings is another great veil which imagination throws over the soul and by which the Light is lost. Also, people inherit their belief from parents and ancestors and follow it blindly, too negligent to know and see for themselves.

order.why: Hear the appeal to forefathers in the selected passage.
Consider the refusal of what is absent from inherited books.
shortened: Whenever I expound to them the mysteries of Thy knowledge and the gems of Thy wisdom, they say "We find not this in the books of our forefathers."

order.why: Apply the challenge within the community of the Bayan.
Read belief and denial mediated through leaders’ eyes.
Keep the explicit rejection of another’s verdict as one’s own.
Hear the reported criticism of controlling religious leadership.
Consider the consequences of treating reputation as a standard.
shortened: Thus in every age the masses, putting their trust in their leaders and clergy, have risen up to deny and harm the truth and its chosen ones. They have supposed that the actions of famous people are the standard, and that imitating any scholar or learned person leads to divine good pleasure.

order.why: Read the reported examples of asking opponents to define a Prophet.
Place the critique within the recurring encounter with revelation.
Preserve the Báb’s severe description in its polemical setting.
Read insight through response to the Manifestation in this text.
Keep the particular judgment in its source context.
Retain the reported characterization without generalizing it to people today.
Read light and veiling in the scriptural interpretation.
shortened: Verily that light (i.e., the Light of the Manifestation) shone forth from the horizon of the Manifestation, appeared upon the horizon of existence, and the darkness was changed into light; the Sun of Guidance dawned in the horizon of heaven, whereby the eyes which were looking unto the Kingdom of God were illuminated, the breasts which were filled with God's love were dilated, and the heavenly spirits were attracted by the magnet of the Holy Spirit, so that the hearts became as pure mirrors reflecting the godlike appearances and manifesting the heavenly lights--except the eyes which were in the veil of imitation of the forefathers (i.e., those who followed the theories of their fathers) were hindered from or veiled from witnessing that brilliant and godlike illumination, and the people held to the superstitions of the Pharisees and neglected the mystery of God and the glad-tidings (recorded) in the Holy Scriptures, which elucidated the appearance of the Lord of Hosts in the promised day.

order.why: Distinguish familiarity with a tradition from recognition of its spiritual purpose.
Examine the historically situated contrast concerning proof and assertion.
Consider the effect of presenting religion as opposed to reason.
Read the report’s explanation of French religious history as an attributed claim.
Keep the warning about opposing forms of excess.
Extend the question of imitation to political and national aspirations.
Connect ignorance and imitation with the injury of war.
Read the clouds of imitation as a cause of conflict.
Keep the brief attribution of religious differences.
Consider the proposed relation between investigation and unity.
Place release from imitation within the wider program of principles.
Examine the reported image of repeatedly rebuilt cobwebs.
Read the condition of clinging without result.
shortened: Observe how people are drowning in the sea of imitation, having no insight of their own. They cling to whatever they have heard, while for thousands of years they have been submerged in the ocean of vain imaginings without finding any result, and they are still asleep.

order.why: Keep the reported description of persistent attachment.
Let the short question interrupt complacency.
Consider how imagined objects of worship can replace spiritual reality.
shortened: O worshipper of truth! People worship their idle fancies, immerse themselves in imitation and are entirely alienated from the hidden secrets of God.

order.why: Read the contrast between apparent and firm supports.
shortened: They are immersed in a sea of blind imitation and have cast away the secrets of your Lord, the All-Glorified. They have firmly clung to the weakest cords and left the firm cord, the 'Urvatu'l-Vuthqa; holding fast to misconceptions which are weaker than spider's web.

order.why: Keep the loss of the garden of unity in view.
shortened: It hath become clear that ye are ravens who have learned the ways of the nightingale. Ye wander in the realm of fancy and imitation, deprived of the blessed garden of unity.

order.why: Consider the inherited imaginings that obstruct recognition.
Hear the challenge to give reasons rather than repeat an answer.
shortened: And when asked "By what proof have you turned away from God?" they say what their forefathers said before. These are indeed among the people of error.

order.why: Retain the brief observation concerning complaints.
shortened: Some complaints have occurred and continue to occur due to blind imitation.

order.why: Notice the warning that imitation can begin again.
Read the cost borne by one who breaks its chains.
shortened: They imprison him who has broken the chains of blind imitation by the hand of divine decree, and they object to him who calls them to the pure wine of divine unity from the cup of the bounty of their Lord, the All-Knowing, the Most Generous.

order.why: Turn from diagnosis toward release.
shortened: Beware lest the conditions of blind imitation prevent thee from the Dayspring of divine unity. Break asunder the chains of idle fancy through this Name whereby the horizon of certitude hath shone forth.

order.why: Connect certitude with the open space of detachment.
shortened: God willing, We hope you will break the chains of imitation with the strength of certitude and enter the pleasant expanse of detachment.

order.why: Read the blessing on a soul no longer restrained by inherited limits.
Keep the particular blessing on a parent and son.
Let release lead to speaking in remembrance.
Hear the testimony of those who have broken the chains.
shortened: We are servants who have shattered the chains of blind imitation through the Most Great Name of God and have detached ourselves from those who disbelieved in Him in Whom they had believed, whose eyes were covered with the veils of idle fancy and who were among the heedless.

order.why: Read the connection between release and true unity.
Keep the brief direct summons to break the chains.
shortened: Break the chains of blind imitation through My Name, the All-Powerful over creation.

order.why: Contrast refusal with a response of certitude.
shortened: We called all to the Path - among the people were those who clung to vain imaginings, turning away from God, the Lord of all mankind, and among them were those who broke the chains of blind imitation and hastened unto Him with clear certitude.

order.why: Read adherence to the revealed Book within its particular claim of authority.
Make freedom from self and passion part of the search.
Connect the revealed light with release from multiple prejudices.
Allow the brief image of dispersing darkness.
Read the age as a summons to discovery.
Carry inquiry toward the unity of East and West.
Close with communities growing together as a garden and an ocean.

questions: How can you distinguish learning from another person from handing over responsibility for your own judgment?
Which forms of imitation are easiest to notice in others and hardest to recognize in yourself?
How do the passages connect unexamined belief with prejudice and conflict?
What does the Kalama Sutta add by examining the fruits of a teaching as well as the authority behind it?
How can independent inquiry remain receptive to revelation, evidence, and correction without becoming mere personal preference?
What practical encounters across religious or cultural boundaries could deepen the understanding encouraged here?

references.label: 1 · Kalama Sutta, AN 3.65, sections 3–15 · Examining claims and their fruits
references.note: In Soma Thera’s translation, the Kalamas face rival teachers’ claims. The Buddha warns against relying merely on repetition, tradition, apparent authority, or favored reasoning, and directs attention to what is recognized as harmful or beneficial, with the judgment of the wise also considered. Greed, hatred, and delusion provide concrete tests. Compare this ethical discernment with the compilation’s call to investigate; neither passage makes personal preference alone a sufficient standard.
